plan: Ten new items, every topic and choice set checked against the live bank (reticent, mantis shrimp, a city-name punctuation set and a parentheses item were dropped as overlapping 151, existing mantis-shrimp items, 266/288/308, and 082). nascent/unassuming WIC, Velcro sentence function, original literary central idea, seedling-distance data, cuttlefish self-control inference, dog 'guilty look' cross-text, Golden Records synthesis, parallel verbs, 'whose'. Key 'whose' differs from 099 (key 'whom'). Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: S036-03 medium→easy, S036-04 medium→easy, S036-06 hard→easy, S036-07 hard→easy, S036-10 medium→easy.

passages.title: Early automobiles
passages.text: In 1900, the American automobile industry was still ______: only about eight thousand cars were registered in the entire country, and most were built by hand in small workshops.

passages.title: A modest architect
passages.text: Although she designed several of the city's best-known buildings, the architect was notably ______: she drove an old car, ate lunch with the junior drafters, and credited her colleagues whenever her work won an award.

passages.title: Burrs and fasteners
passages.text: In 1941, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral returned from a walk to find burrs clinging to his trousers and to his dog's fur. Curious, he examined a burr under a microscope and saw that it was covered in tiny hooks that caught on anything with loops, such as fabric or hair. It took him years to reproduce the effect with woven nylon. The result, a fastener made of one strip of hooks and one of loops, was patented in the 1950s under the name Velcro.

passages.title: The new coat
passages.text:
The following text is from an original short story. Ana has just received a winter coat from her older sister, Marisol.
The coat was the deep green of pine needles, and it still smelled faintly of Marisol's perfume. One cuff had been carefully mended with thread that almost matched. Ana had wanted a new coat all autumn, one with shiny buttons that no one else had worn. Now she turned the green coat over in her hands, found the mended cuff, and pictured her sister bent over it late at night. She put the coat on and did not take it off for the rest of the day.

passages.title: Seedlings and parent trees
passages.text:
In one tropical forest, researchers tracked the survival of seedlings of a single tree species for two years, grouping them by distance from the nearest adult tree of the same species.
Distance from adult tree | Seedlings that survived two years
0–5 meters | 12%
5–20 meters | 35%
More than 20 meters | 51%
The researchers concluded that seedlings growing close to an adult of their own species are less likely to survive than seedlings growing farther away.

passages.title: Patient cuttlefish
passages.text: Researchers offered common cuttlefish a choice: a piece of king prawn available right away, or a live grass shrimp, which cuttlefish prefer, that would be released only after a delay. Many cuttlefish ignored the prawn and waited for the shrimp, some for more than a minute. The cuttlefish that waited longest also learned a separate task more quickly than the others did. Because self-control and learning ability seemed to go together in these animals, the researchers suggested that ______

passages.title: The guilty look (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Many dog owners report that their dogs look "guilty"—lowering their heads, avoiding eye contact, and tucking their tails—after doing something forbidden. To many owners, this look shows that dogs know when they have broken a rule.
Text 2
In a 2009 study, psychologist Alexandra Horowitz told owners to forbid their dogs from eating a treat and then leave the room. Sometimes the dogs ate the treat; sometimes the researcher secretly removed it. Owners were then told, sometimes falsely, that their dog had eaten it. Dogs showed the most "guilty" behavior when their owners scolded them, whether or not the dog had actually eaten the treat.

passages.title: The Golden Records
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft were launched in 1977.
• Each carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record.
• The records contain greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds, music, and 115 images encoded in sound.
• They were intended as a message to any intelligent beings who might someday find the spacecraft.
• Both spacecraft have since left the region of space dominated by the solar wind.

passages.title: A helpful robot
passages.text: The warehouse robot can climb short flights of stairs, open doors with a gripper arm, and ______ packages weighing up to twenty kilograms.

passages.title: Discovering a signal
passages.text: The astronomer ______ team first detected the repeating radio signal was initially reluctant to announce the finding until other observatories had confirmed it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: only about eight thousand cars were registered
candidates.explanation: Few cars and handmade production in small workshops describe an industry that had only just begun: "nascent."

A.rationale: An industry that had barely begun was not out of date.

C.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns rules or regulation.

D.rationale: Many small workshops suggest the industry was scattered, not combined into a few large firms.

hints: Was the industry just starting or well established?
candidates.remember: Details after a colon usually define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: credited her colleagues whenever her work won an award
candidates.explanation: Despite her success, she lived and worked without show or self-importance: "unassuming."

A.rationale: Sharing credit and avoiding display do not show ambition.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests she had trouble making decisions.

C.rationale: An old car and lunch with junior staff are the opposite of extravagant.

hints: How did she behave despite her fame?
candidates.remember: "Although" signals that the blank contrasts with her success.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains what de Mestral discovered about why the burrs stuck, which became the basis for his invention.
choices.B: It describes the difficulties de Mestral faced in reproducing the burr's effect with manufactured materials.
choices.C: It introduces the walk during which de Mestral first noticed the burrs on his clothes and his dog.
choices.D: It identifies the name under which the finished fastener was eventually patented in the 1950s.

candidates.evidence: covered in tiny hooks that caught on anything with loops
candidates.explanation: The second sentence reveals the hook-and-loop mechanism, which the last sentence shows became the design of the fastener.

B.rationale: Those difficulties appear in the third sentence.

C.rationale: The walk is described in the first sentence.

D.rationale: The name appears in the last sentence.

hints: What does the second sentence reveal?
candidates.remember: Function questions ask what a sentence does in the text as a whole.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Ana is disappointed that her sister gave her a coat that had already been worn and repaired.
choices.B: Ana decides to mend the coat's damaged cuff herself, more neatly, before she will agree to wear it.
choices.C: Ana's wish for a new coat gives way to appreciation once she sees the care her sister put into the old one.
choices.D: Ana realizes that the coat is too large for her and will need to be altered by her sister.

candidates.evidence: pictured her sister bent over it late at night
candidates.explanation: Ana had wanted a new coat, but noticing the carefully mended cuff and picturing Marisol's work, she puts it on and keeps it on, showing that her feelings change.

A.rationale: Ana wears the coat all day after imagining Marisol mending it, which shows appreciation, not disappointment.

B.rationale: Marisol has already mended the cuff; Ana does not repair anything.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text suggests the coat does not fit.

hints: How does Ana's attitude change, and why?

strategy.explanation: Compare the beginning and the end.

candidates.remember: A literary main idea usually involves a change in a character.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Survival was 35% for seedlings growing between 5 and 20 meters from an adult tree.
choices.B: Fewer than half of the seedlings within 20 meters of an adult tree survived two years.
choices.C: About half of the seedlings growing more than 20 meters from an adult tree survived.
choices.D: Survival rose from 12% within 5 meters of an adult tree to 51% more than 20 meters away.

candidates.evidence: seedlings growing close to an adult of their own species are less likely to survive
candidates.explanation: The conclusion compares near and far seedlings; D shows survival rising from 12% at 0–5 meters to 51% beyond 20 meters.

A.rationale: This gives one value and does not compare near and far seedlings.

B.rationale: This describes only the nearer groups and makes no comparison with seedlings farther away.

C.rationale: This gives only the farthest group's rate, with nothing to compare it to.

hints: What two groups does the conclusion compare?

strategy.explanation: Find the comparison in the claim.

candidates.remember: A comparison claim needs data from both groups.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: cuttlefish cannot reliably tell the difference between king prawn and live grass shrimp.
choices.B: the capacity to delay a reward may be linked to how well cuttlefish learn, not only to how they feed.
choices.C: cuttlefish that eat the prawn immediately are unable to learn any new tasks at all.
choices.D: waiting for food is harmful to cuttlefish because the delay lowers their later ability to learn.

candidates.evidence: The cuttlefish that waited longest also learned a separate task more quickly
candidates.explanation: The longest waiters also learned fastest, so the researchers suggest self-control and learning ability may be connected.

A.rationale: The cuttlefish waited specifically for the shrimp they prefer, so they can tell the foods apart.

C.rationale: The text says the patient cuttlefish learned faster, not that others could not learn at all.

D.rationale: The patient cuttlefish learned more quickly, the opposite of harm to learning.

strategy.explanation: Combine the last two findings before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: An inference must follow from the evidence without overstating it.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Horowitz most likely respond to the owners' view described in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the "guilty" look appears to be a response to the owner's scolding rather than evidence that a dog knows it broke a rule
choices.B: By agreeing that the look shows dogs know when they have broken a rule, since dogs who ate the treat looked most guilty
choices.C: By arguing that dogs never show any special behavior after their owners leave the room
choices.D: By suggesting that owners should stop forbidding their dogs from eating treats in the home

candidates.evidence: whether or not the dog had actually eaten the treat
candidates.explanation: Text 2 found the look tracked scolding, even when the dog had done nothing wrong, so Horowitz would say it reflects the owner's behavior rather than the dog's knowledge of wrongdoing.

B.rationale: In Text 2 the look depended on scolding, not on whether the dog had eaten the treat.

C.rationale: Text 2 reports guilty behavior; it does not say dogs show no special behavior.

D.rationale: Text 2 makes no recommendation about household rules.

hints: What predicted the guilty look in Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Identify the claim in Text 1, then the finding in Text 2.

candidates.remember: Cross-text questions ask how one text's evidence bears on the other's claim.

candidates.stem: The student wants to introduce the Golden Records to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The records contain spoken greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds, a selection of music, and 115 images encoded in sound.
choices.B: Both Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, have since traveled beyond the region of space dominated by the solar wind.
choices.C: Launched aboard the Voyager spacecraft in 1977, the Golden Records carry sounds, music, and images meant for any intelligent beings who find them.
choices.D: Each of the two Voyager spacecraft carries a gold-plated copper record intended as a message to any intelligent beings.

candidates.evidence: They were intended as a message to any intelligent beings
candidates.explanation: An introduction for an unfamiliar audience should say what the records are, where they are, what they hold, and why; C does all four.

A.rationale: This lists contents without saying what the records are or where they are.

B.rationale: This is about the spacecraft, not the records.

D.rationale: This mentions the records and their purpose but not what they contain, which an unfamiliar audience would need.

hints: What would someone who has never heard of the records need to know?

strategy.explanation: List what an introduction needs, then check each choice.

candidates.remember: Match the choice to the audience named in the goal.

candidates.subskill: Parallel structure in a series of verbs
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: can climb short flights of stairs, open doors
candidates.explanation: All three actions follow "can": "can climb..., open..., and carry...." The base form keeps the series parallel.

A.rationale: The other verbs in the series (climb, open) are base forms after "can," so the third must be too.

B.rationale: "To carry" breaks the series of base-form verbs that follow "can."

C.rationale: Adding a subject and verb breaks the parallel series.

hints: What form are the first two verbs?

strategy.explanation: Match the form of the other items.

candidates.remember: Items in a series must share the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: team first detected the repeating radio signal
candidates.explanation: The team belongs to the astronomer, so the possessive relative pronoun "whose" is needed.

B.rationale: "Who's" means "who is," which makes no sense before "team."

C.rationale: "Who" cannot show that the team belongs to the astronomer.

D.rationale: "Whom" is an object pronoun and cannot show possession.

hints: Does the team belong to the astronomer?
